entries.propagation_note: A records typically propagate within 5 minutes. Some resolvers may cache up to the TTL value.
AAAA records follow the same propagation pattern as A records.
MX record changes may take up to 1 hour to propagate. Mail delivery may be affected during transition.
TXT records (including SPF) typically propagate within 1 hour. Verify with multiple resolvers.
Nameserver changes can take 24–48 hours for full global propagation due to parent zone TTLs.
CNAME changes propagate quickly but downstream records inherit the CNAME TTL.
CAA record changes take effect within TTL. Certificate authorities check at issuance time.
SOA changes propagate to secondaries based on the Refresh interval in the SOA record.
SPF record changes propagate within the TXT record TTL. Test with dig before relying on scan results.
DMARC policy changes at _dmarc subdomain propagate within TTL. Reporting changes take 24–48h to reflect in aggregate reports.
DKIM selector records propagate within TTL. New selectors are available immediately once published; key rotation requires overlap period.
MTA-STS policy changes require updating both the DNS TXT record AND the policy file at /.well-known/mta-sts.txt. The max_age directive in the policy controls how long senders cache it.
TLS-RPT changes propagate within TTL. Report delivery changes take effect in the next reporting period (typically 24 hours).
BIMI record changes propagate within TTL. VMC certificate validation by mail providers may take additional time.
TLSA/DANE records must be published BEFORE rotating TLS certificates. Premature certificate rotation breaks DANE validation.
DNSSEC signing changes (DS record updates at registrar) can take 24–48 hours. Key rollovers require careful timing per RFC 7583.
DANE/TLSA record updates follow the TLSA TTL. Coordinate with TLS certificate lifecycle.

results.title: SPF Effective Authorization Policy
results.fail_explanation: SPF policy is permissive without DMARC enforcement. SPF softfail (~all) without DMARC p=reject or p=quarantine leaves email authorization unenforced. Per RFC 7489, DMARC provides the enforcement layer that makes SPF softfail operationally effective. Either tighten SPF to -all or deploy DMARC with an enforcement policy.

weakness_refs.mapping_rationale: Permissive SPF without DMARC enforcement lets a forged sender bypass origin authentication (CWE-290) by faking the source domain (CAPEC-194/151). SPF is contributory, so confidence is medium; VRT files this failure mode under the DMARC entry. CWE/CAPEC verified against MITRE.

results.title: DMARC Policy Enforcement
results.fail_explanation: DMARC policy is not set to reject. Per RFC 7489 §6.3, only p=reject instructs receivers to discard unauthenticated messages. NIST SP 800-177 Rev. 1 §4.6.1 recommends reject for all production domains.

weakness_refs.mapping_rationale: p=none and p=quarantine do not instruct receivers to reject unauthenticated mail, so sender authentication is effectively bypassed (CWE-290), enabling domain identity spoofing (CAPEC-151), forged-source mail (CAPEC-194) and spear phishing (CAPEC-163). This is the flagship false-green-checkmark gap: tools mark DMARC present as compliant while the domain remains spoofable. Mapping verified against MITRE CWE/CAPEC and Bugcrowd VRT.

results.title: DKIM Signature Availability
results.fail_explanation: DKIM not discoverable for this mail-sending domain. Per RFC 6376, DKIM provides cryptographic proof of message origin. Without DKIM, email from this domain cannot be cryptographically verified by receivers.

results.title: CAA Certificate Issuance Restriction
results.fail_explanation: No CAA records found — any Certificate Authority can issue certificates for this domain. Per RFC 8659 §4.2, CAs are required to check CAA records before issuance. Without CAA, misissued certificates cannot be prevented at the DNS layer.

posture.deliberate_monitoring_note: DMARC is published at p=none with aggregate reporting enabled (RFC 7489 §6.3) — authentication results are reported but no enforcement is requested. The domain separately deploys a validating DNSSEC chain and BIMI, so an unfinished rollout is the less likely reading. It's possible this organization is deliberately prioritising observation over enforcement. What this means if you receive mail from this domain: p=none blocks nothing — a spoofed message that fails authentication is delivered to the inbox exactly as it would be with no DMARC record at all. Moving to quarantine or reject adds protection while aggregate reporting continues unchanged.
